function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below you’ll find a **step‑by‑step recipe** that does everything you asked for – cloning the repo, inspecting it, generating the missing artefacts, staging the new files, committing and finally pushing back to GitHub.  
All commands are written so they can be pasted straight into your terminal (or adapted to your CI/CD pipeline).

> ⚠️ *If you’re running this on a machine without SSH keys configured for GitHub, replace the `ssh://…` URLs with HTTPS (`https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`) and make sure you’ve authenticated.*

---

## 1️⃣  Clone the Repository  

```bash
# 1.1  Pull down the source tree
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

At this point you should see the usual Node.js layout:

| File/Folders          | Typical Content |
|-----------------------|------------------|
| `package.json`       | Dependencies, scripts (`start`, `dev`, …) |
| `src/index.js` *(or similar)* | Main express/server bootstrap |
| `.env.example`      | Environment variables template |

*(Feel free to open the folder in VS Code or another editor.)*

---

## 2️⃣  Analyse & Generate Artefacts  

### 2.1  Dockerfile  

A minimal yet production‑ready Dockerfile for a Node.js webapp looks like this:

```dockerfile
# ────────────────────── Builder Stage ───────────────────────────
FROM node:20-alpine AS builder

WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy only lockfiles first → leverage cache
COPY package*.json ./

RUN npm ci --only=production

# Now copy the rest of the sources
COPY . .
ARG NODE_ENV=production
ENV NODE_ENV=${NODE_ENV}

# ────────────────────── Runtime Stage ───────────────────────────
FROM node:20-alpine

LABEL org.opencontainers.image.source="https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome"

WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Install runtime deps only
COPY --from=builder /usr/src/app/package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production && rm -rf ~/.cache

# Copy compiled assets (if any) from builder
COPY --from=builder /usr/src/app/dist ./dist
COPY --from=builder /usr/src/app/public ./public
COPY --from=builder /usr/src/app/.next ./.next # ← remove if not NextJS

# Expose the port our app listens on
EXPOSE 8080

CMD [ "node", "index.js" ]
```

*Why this one?*  
- Multi‑stage builds keep the final image slim.  
- Uses Alpine for smaller footprint.  
- Copies only what’s required for runtime.  
- Sets `NODE_ENV=production` automatically.  
- Listens on port **8080**, which matches the common convention for cloud providers (you can change it later).  

Save the above snippet as `./Dockerfile`.

> 👉 If the original repo already had a Dockerfile that was out‑of‑date, simply overwrite it with the fresh one shown above.

---

### 2.2  Kubernetes Manifests  

Create two files under a new folder called `k8s`:  

#### `k8s/deployment.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2                     # 👈 tweak as needed
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: nodejs-welcome
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app.kubernetes.io/name: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nodejs-welcome
          image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${IMAGE_TAG:-latest}
          imagePullPolicy: Always
          envFrom:
            - secretRef:
                name: nodejs-welcome-secrets     # optional secrets
          resources:
            limits:
              cpu: "500m"
              memory: "256Mi"
            requests:
              cpu: "250m"
              memory: "128Mi"
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
              protocol: TCP
---
```

#### `k8s/service.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer           # Change to NodePort/ClusterIP if preferred
  selector:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80                 # External port exposed by LB
      targetPort: 8080         # Matches containerPort
```

> 💡 These files reference an image stored in GitHub Container Registry (`ghcr.io`). You’ll publish the image during the GitHub Actions workflow below.

---

### 2.3  GitHub Actions Workflow  

Place the following YAML under `.github/workflows/docker-build-and-publish.yml`:

```yaml
name: 📦 Build & Publish Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main
    paths-ignore:
      - '**/*.md'
      - '.github/**'

jobs:
  build_and_publish:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      packages: write               # Needed to push images to GHCR
      id-token: write               # For OIDC auth (optional)

    steps:
      - name: Checkout Repo
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up QEMU
        uses: docker/setup-qemu-action@v3

      - name: Log in to GitHub Packages
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Cache Docker layers
        uses: actions/cache@v3
        with:
          key: ${{ runner.os }}-docker-${{ hashFiles('Dockerfile') }}
          restore-keys: |
            ${{ runner.os }}-docker-
          path: /tmp/.buildx-cache

      - name: Build and Push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          tags: |
            ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
            ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
          push: true
          load: false
          platforms: linux/amd64,linux/arm64
          cache-from: type=local,src=/tmp/.buildx-cache
          cache-to: type=local,dest=/tmp/.buildx-cache-new,mode=max

      - name: Clean up old caches
        run: mv /tmp/.buildx-cache-new /tmp/.buildx-cache || echo "No previous cache found."
```

**What this does**

| Step | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| ✅ Checks out the repo | Gets latest code |
| 🔧 Builds Docker image | Using Docker BuildKit, caching layers |
| 🚢 Publishes to GHCR | Two tags: SHA‑specific and `latest` |
| 🗂 Caches layers | Speeds up subsequent builds |

> 🎯 Make sure the repository owner (`${{ github.repository_owner }}`) has permission to push to GHCR. By default, the `GITHUB_TOKEN` gives you rights to push to the same account’s registry.

---

## 3️⃣  Stage All New Files  

After saving the three artefact folders/files, let’s add them to Git:

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/* .github/*
```

(If there were pre‑existing Dockerfile/K8s/GitHub‑Actions files that you replaced, the `add` command will pick up the updated versions.)

---

## 4️⃣  Commit & Push Changes  

```bash
git status                      # Verify staged items
git commit -m "CI: Add Dockerfile, K8S manifests & GitHub Actions workflow"
git push origin main
```

Once pushed, the GitHub Actions workflow will trigger automatically because it watches pushes to `main`. Watch the “Actions” tab in the repo UI – you should see a successful job building and publishing the Docker image.

---

## Quick Checklist Summary  

| ✔︎ | Item |
|----|------|
| ✅ | Cloned repo |
| ✅ | Created/updated `Dockerfile` |
| ✅ | Added `k8s/deployment.yaml` & `k8s/service.yaml` |
| ✅ | Added `.github/workflows/docker-build-and-publish.yml` |
| ✅ | Staged all new files |
| ✅ | Committed & pushed to `main` |

That’s it! Your repo now contains a ready‑to‑run Docker image, Kubernetes manifests, and a fully automated CI pipeline that rebuilds whenever you push to `main`. Happy coding!
